## The Revival, 2018–2020

Every retrospective of the Vanguard Circuit arrives eventually at the same comfortable story: the game was saved by its corporate patrons. A streaming deal here, a steep digital sale there, and the audience returned. It is a tidy account, and it is backwards.

The Circuit's considered position is this: the commercial rebirth of the game was generated from below, by Project Aegis — the volunteer-run tournament network — and the corporate milestones of 2019 were not its cause but its consequence. The industry did not rescue the game. It noticed that the game had already been rescued, and moved to profit from a revival it did not create.

The chronology is the argument. [INSERT: date] — eight months before the streaming deal was announced — the player surge had already begun. [INSERT: server growth figures, e.g. concurrent-player or registration logs across the Aegis period]. The deal did not precede the recovery; it followed it. Any account that places the corporate milestone first is not describing a cause. It is describing an after-effect.

What produced that surge was not a marketing budget. It was labor. Project Aegis was built by organizers who were paid nothing and owed nothing — [INSERT: organizer names/count, e.g. "a core of N volunteers across M regions"] — and who ran tournaments on their own time, on their own servers, for the sake of the game. [INSERT: organizer testimony — a direct quote or two carries this paragraph further than any statistic]. Their work did not merely accompany the revival. It constituted it.

The corporate milestones, on this reading, are epiphenomena: real, visible, and dependent. The streaming deal gave the revival a wider stage. The digital sale gave it a price point. Neither gave it a reason to exist. That reason was already there, in the brackets and the back channels, before any of it was monetized.

This is the Circuit's thesis, and we state it plainly: the game's commercial rebirth was authored by its players, and the industry arrived late to a party it did not throw.

## Timeline: The Aegis Years

**Primary entries — Project Aegis**

- **[DATE] — Network launch.** Project Aegis goes live as a volunteer-run tournament network. [INSERT: founding organizers, initial scope — regions, game version, platform]
- **[DATE] — First cross-regional finals.** The network's first finals drawing competitors from more than one region. [INSERT: entrant count, regions represented, winner or notable result]
- **[DATE] — Server growth inflection.** The point at which player growth stops being linear and starts compounding. [INSERT: the figures — this is the entry the whole sidebar is built to support]

**Subordinate entries — dependent developments**

- ↳ **[DATE] — Anime streaming deal announced.** Follows the growth inflection by eight months. [INSERT: exact interval, and the deal's own date]
- ↳ **[DATE] — Digital sale.** [INSERT: discount depth, duration, and any sales figures]

A few notes on the structure:

- **The indentation does the argument.** Primary entries sit flush left; subordinate entries are marked with ↳ and indented. A reader absorbs the causal claim from the layout before reading a word of it — which is exactly what you want from a sidebar.
- **The eight-month interval is the hinge.** I've written it into the streaming-deal entry as a cross-reference back to the inflection. That's the one place the sidebar states the relationship outright rather than implying it through position. If the interval is your strongest number, consider setting it in bold or as a pull-quote.
- **The subordinate entries still need dates.** They're dependent, not undated. A reader who sees "↳ Anime streaming deal" with no date will assume you couldn't find one.
- **One structural caution:** if the digital sale predates the growth inflection, the hierarchy will read as forced and a sharp reader will notice. Worth checking the dates against each other before typesetting.

- **The closing clauses are doing real work, so they need to be true.** "Did not initiate the revival" and "did not create the demand" are claims about causation, and they're the kind of sentence a critic will quote back at you. If your archive supports them, they're strong.
